commenti.body:
Thank you so much for these translations. I understand Ohii's perspective, even if I don't entirely agree, but more importantly I really appreciate how deeply he understands the artform. Really great stuff.

I'd be interested in what he thinks of Ponyo - though I expect he'll criticise the lacking coherency of a grand theme again - surely he won't be able to doubt the vibrancy of the animation. Every scene in Ponyo just looks fantastic.

Bingo, let me give you the rundown on Oshii’s thoughts about Ponyo.

*Right off the bat, you've got those underwater sequences, and then there’s that part with the submerged city where ancient fish are just gliding around. It's classic Miyazaki. Seriously impressive stuff – technically brilliant. Nobody else can conjure those kinds of visuals. Miyazaki's imagination just runs wild; it's a real 'Miyazaki Spectacular.'*

*The problem is, the visuals take on a life of their own, almost to the point where it all becomes unmanageable. That’s a big reason why the story feels so disjointed. Ponyo's visuals are so overpowering that the narrative can't keep pace. In the end, it can’t even manage to tell a coherent story.*
No coherent story? Buddy you made ghost in the shell
Which is more coherent than some of Miyazaki's films, the story of the original Ghost in the Shell isn't that complex and is coherent.

>"it's as always a film where scenes he wanted to create are string together"

I find this is the case for many great directors and great films, I find it to be a peculiar basis for criticism. To me this kind of storytelling makes great cinema and is what separates it from longer form modes of storytelling like television or miniseries. What can the director conjure and elucidate from the sequence and proximity of scenes which on their own are also captivating and evocative.
i was anticipating this reply which is why i've got a perfect rejoinder: "...2: Innocence"

Innocence is also not a complex plot, its just got a lot of philosophical text in the script that seems to make people think its a lot more complex than it actually is.

>!Yakuza are kidnapping young girls for a company to dub their ghosts onto the sex dolls, one person realises what's happening in the company and messes with the process so they start murdering people to draw attention to the company, he gets killed by the Yakuza.<!

That's the plot, and apart from the sci-fi elements, you might see something like that in a police procedural. Everything makes sense within the film too and I'm glad Innocence is finally getting reevaluated by some.

so it‘s not just me that derives a lot of satisfaction and contentment from watching these eating scenes, as odd as it may seem. 

is there additional meaning to haku‘s rice ball? I can’t remember the scene at all, it’s been a very long time.

thanks for the interview, great insight into the mind of an expert in his field
We’re comparing Oshii and Miyazaki right now, and the relative coherence of their plots. My initial reply was in the context of a quote of his about Ponyo.
Neither Ghost in the Shell has an incohesive plot. They're fairly basic, tbh. It's the themes that are very intricate.
cohesive and coherent are different words and, again, i am responding to his quote about *ponyo.*
